intro: The medicine of human spaceflight is the discipline of managing five hazards—changes in gravity, distance from Earth, radiation, isolation and confinement, and hostile/closed environments—through countermeasures and operations.
lessons.0.title: The Five Hazards Map All Symptoms
lessons.0.summary: Before memorizing individual disease names, prioritize the five threats officially grouped by NASA.
lessons.0.body.0: NASA's Human Research Program and related technical reports organize the threats of human spaceflight into five categories: changing gravity fields, distance from Earth, radiation, isolation and confinement, and hostile/closed environments. Under each hazard hang multiple risks, such as bone, eye, behavioral health, infection, and fire.
lessons.0.body.1: The weight of these five hazards changes in Low Earth Orbit (ISS), on the Moon, and on Mars. Distance becomes critical on the Moon, radiation is significant outside the magnetic field, and gravity involves a continuum of microgravity, 1/6 G, and readaptation. The 180-day health management minigame is designed for long-duration ISS stays, allocating exercise and nutrition.
lessons.0.body.2: The division of labor between the flight surgeon and the crew differs from that in a terrestrial hospital. Diagnostic equipment is limited, and return is not immediate. Therefore, daily measurements—body weight, blood pressure, vision, mood, and exercise load—serve as early detection of abnormalities.
lessons.0.facts.0.label: Framework
lessons.0.facts.1.label: Context
lessons.0.deepDive.title: Distinguish Hazards, Risks, Countermeasures, and Metrics
lessons.0.deepDive.body.0: A hazard is an environmental condition that creates danger, while a risk is the potential impact on health or performance arising from that condition. For example, starting from changes in gravity, one can trace the connection to decreased mineral density in weight-bearing bones, countermeasures involving exercise and nutrition, and pre- and post-flight imaging assessments.
lessons.0.deepDive.body.1: Records of implementing countermeasures differ from records of verifying their effectiveness. The indices in the game are values designed to compare allocation strategies. Do not interpret them as predicted values for bone density or incidence rates; instead, consider what must be measured to judge the effectiveness of countermeasures.
lessons.1.title: Fluids Shift to the Head, Changing Face, Eyes, and Heart
lessons.1.summary: Fluid that pools in the legs on Earth shifts to the chest and head in microgravity.
lessons.1.body.0: NASA's human body explanations state that fluids shift toward the head immediately after launch. Facial puffiness, nasal congestion, and thinner legs are well-known early signs. Plasma volume decreases, and although the heart appears to be processing 'excess blood,' the actual circulating blood volume is readjusted.
lessons.1.body.1: This shift simultaneously affects the next module on eyes (SANS), the heart module, and the vestibular module. Intracranial pressure, inner ear signals, and vision combine in ways that differ from those on Earth.
lessons.1.body.2: Countermeasures do not involve suddenly lowering the head. They include salt and fluid intake, exercise, monitoring, and medication if necessary. After return, fluids shift back to the legs, which can cause orthostatic hypotension. Walking immediately after landing is a trained readaptation process.
lessons.1.facts.0.label: Direction
lessons.1.facts.1.label: Return
lessons.2.title: Bones Release Minerals from Unused Areas
lessons.2.summary: Reduced loading affects bone mineral density, and increased urinary calcium is linked to kidney stone risk.
lessons.2.body.0: In microgravity, bone density in the pelvis, femur, and lumbar vertebrae, which are loaded during walking, decreases. NASA's human body explanations state that the mineral density of weight-bearing bones decreases by an average of 1–1.5% per month during spaceflight. This is not a prediction for individuals and varies depending on countermeasures and measurement sites. Lost calcium is excreted in urine, increasing the risk of kidney stones.
lessons.2.body.1: The primary countermeasure is resistance exercise. The ISS's ARED (Advanced Resistive Exercise Device) generates loads equivalent to squats and deadlifts using vacuum cylinders. The second is nutrition including Vitamin D and calcium, and the third is regular bone density assessment.
lessons.2.body.2: In the 180-day plan, do not fill monthly exercise allocations with 'aerobic' exercise alone. What benefits bones is the load that muscles pull on them. Cutting nutrition to maintain weight alone will cause bones to quietly atrophy.
lessons.2.facts.0.label: Weakness
lessons.2.facts.1.label: Countermeasure
lessons.3.title: Anti-gravity Muscles Decline Within Weeks If Unused
lessons.3.summary: The back and leg muscles that support posture are the first to be deemed unnecessary.
lessons.3.body.0: NASA treats muscle atrophy in microgravity as a physical hazard alongside bone loss. In particular, anti-gravity muscles—the soleus, quadriceps, and erector spinae—decline. Not only strength, but also endurance and coordination change. EVA glove work causes muscle fatigue patterns that differ from those on Earth.
lessons.3.body.1: Countermeasures combine aerobic (T2 treadmill, cycle) and resistance exercise. In official long-duration operations, daily exercise time is central to life. Verify load settings and consistency, and share any excessive fatigue or malaise with the medical team.
lessons.3.body.2: Health management in the mini-game requires monitoring four gauges simultaneously: bone, muscle, cardiopulmonary, and recovery. A plan that maximizes only one is a failure.
lessons.3.facts.0.label: Priority Sites
lessons.3.facts.1.label: Devices
lessons.4.title: The heart reshapes itself to match a relaxed circulation
lessons.4.summary: When fluid shifts and inactivity overlap, cardiac output and autonomic responses diverge from ground conditions.
lessons.4.body.0: In microgravity, the heart's workload changes, causing myocardial mass and shape to readapt. NASA's human body explanations treat post-flight orthostatic intolerance as a failure of circulatory readaptation. Even if 'fine' in orbit, vision may darken upon standing in 1G.
lessons.4.body.1: Exercise is also a countermeasure for the heart. Aerobic activity preserves maximum oxygen uptake, while resistance exercise protects the leg pump involved in venous return. Salt and fluid plans are particularly emphasized the day before return.
lessons.4.body.2: Measurements include resting heart rate, exercise load, and ultrasound if necessary. Report any arrhythmia complaints to the Surgeon and CAPCOM without hesitation. Heroic endurance earns no points in circulation.
lessons.4.facts.0.label: In Orbit
lessons.4.facts.1.label: Return
lessons.5.title: The eye has become one of the most scrutinized organs in spaceflight
lessons.5.summary: Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome includes changes in the optic nerve and eye shape.
lessons.5.body.0: NASA's human body and HRP reports have noted that some long-duration crew experience eye flattening, optic disc edema, and refractive changes. The general term is SANS. Fluid shift toward the head and the pressure relationship between intracranial and intraocular spaces are central to leading hypotheses.
lessons.5.body.1: It does not occur with the same severity in everyone. Therefore, vision, fundus, and optical measurements are taken regularly. Changes may start with 'slight blurring,' and ground-based glasses prescriptions may no longer fit.
lessons.5.body.2: NASA is investigating the relationship between fluid shifts and visual changes, and researching countermeasures such as devices to return fluid to the lower body. Research challenges remain regarding SANS mechanisms and countermeasures. It is important to record symptoms and measurements for evaluation by the medical team.
lessons.5.facts.0.label: Example Findings
lessons.5.facts.1.label: Principle
lessons.6.title: The brain and vestibular system recalibrate in a world without up or down
lessons.6.summary: Space motion sickness, spatial disorientation, sleep, and mood are at the intersection of isolation hazards and gravity hazards.
lessons.6.body.0: The otoliths in the inner ear lose the gravity vector. Vision and proprioception substitute to create 'up.' Initial space motion sickness is experienced by many crew. Official human body explanations acknowledge that adaptation takes several days while not ignoring the impact on work performance.
lessons.6.body.1: Isolation and confinement are one of the five hazards. The cramped cabin, delayed ground contact, the same faces, and orbital sunrises that cut into sleep. Behavioral health is not a private weakness but a mission risk.
lessons.6.body.2: Countermeasures include sleep plans, lighting, exercise, personal calls, task variety, and early reporting. The vestibular system adapts by avoiding sudden head movements and using medication if necessary. For the brain, journals are more effective than heroic tales.
lessons.6.facts.0.label: Initial
lessons.6.facts.1.label: Long-term
lessons.7.title: Radiation is an invisible but accumulating hazard
lessons.7.summary: Low orbit is protected by the magnetic field and hull. On the Moon and Mars, that shield becomes thinner.
lessons.7.body.0: Radiation is one of the five hazards. Galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events increase long-term risks of DNA damage, cataracts, cardiovascular, and central nervous system issues. The ISS blocks a significant amount via Earth's magnetic field and hull, but it is not zero. Extravehicular activity is an act of leaving the hull's shield.
lessons.7.body.1: Solar particle events become operational decisions spanning hours to days. Check forecasts to delay EVAs and retreat to areas with thicker shielding inside the cabin. On the lunar surface and in deep space, the weight of this decision increases.
lessons.7.body.2: Personal dosimeters, in-cabin monitors, and lifetime dose management determine career length. Medicine is not a subject of 'fear' but one of framing with numbers.
lessons.7.facts.1.label: Deep Space
lessons.8.title: Closed environments are the medicine of air, microbes, and fire
lessons.8.summary: Hostile/closed environment hazards link ECLSS, emergency response, and behavior into one.
lessons.8.body.0: The final of the five hazards is the closed atmosphere itself. Rising carbon dioxide levels can cause headaches and alter cognition, trace pollutants can irritate the eyes and airways, and combustion products from fires can become immediately fatal in a vessel with no escape. Official fire protection guidelines address prevention (using fire-resistant materials), detection, suppression, personal protective equipment, and post-fire atmosphere purification as a continuous sequence.
lessons.8.body.1: Microbes and mold proliferate when humidity and condensation are not properly managed. Wounds may heal differently in microgravity. Changes in the immune system are also tracked as part of the Human Research Program (HRP).
lessons.8.body.2: Medical topics connect to emergency scenarios such as fire, decompression, and ammonia exposure. Here, it is important to understand that daily management of CO2, humidity, and cleaning serves as primary prevention to reduce the need for emergency care.
lessons.8.facts.0.label: Daily
lessons.8.facts.1.label: Extreme
lessons.9.title: 180 Days: A Problem of Allocating Exercise, Nutrition, and Measurement
lessons.9.summary: Countermeasures are not just knowledge; they only become effective when scheduled on a calendar.
lessons.9.body.0: Official human body guidelines designate exercise as a core countermeasure for long-duration missions. This includes resistance training for bones, aerobic training for the heart and lungs, and achievable loads for mental well-being. Nutrition must provide not just calories, but also protein, calcium, Vitamin D, salt, and fiber within a limited menu.
lessons.9.body.1: The mini-game requires players to plan a 180-day schedule in 30-day increments, ensuring that bone, muscle, and cardiovascular gauges do not deteriorate. Consecutive weeks of high-intensity training can lead to injuries that halt exercise entirely. Rest is also a countermeasure.
lessons.9.body.2: Missing measurements are a risk in themselves, as the absence of data is a hazard. Weight, vision, mood, and exercise logs must be recorded in a format visible to the surgeon. Success is not defined by 'getting stronger,' but by ensuring that the crew and ground-based medical teams are looking at the same numbers.
lessons.9.facts.0.label: Pillars
lessons.9.facts.1.label: Failure
quiz.0.prompt: How many primary hazards does NASA organize for human spaceflight?
quiz.0.explanation: The HRP and related reports group hazards into five categories: gravity, distance, radiation, isolation and confinement, and hostile/closed environments.
quiz.1.prompt: In microgravity, which direction do body fluids primarily shift?
quiz.1.explanation: Fluids that pooled in the legs on Earth shift headward, causing facial puffiness and requiring circulatory readjustment.
quiz.2.prompt: Which body parts are particularly problematic for bone density loss during long-duration missions?
quiz.2.choices.0: Only the distal phalanges of the fingers
quiz.2.choices.1: Only the ossicles of the ear
quiz.2.choices.2: Load-bearing areas: hips, legs, and vertebrae
quiz.2.explanation: Bones that previously bore walking loads, such as the pelvis, femur, and lumbar vertebrae, release minerals, increasing urinary calcium excretion and the risk of kidney stones.
quiz.3.prompt: What is the official resistance exercise device on the ISS used to create loads for squats, etc.?
quiz.3.explanation: The Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED) uses vacuum cylinders and other mechanisms to create loads equivalent to resistance, serving as a countermeasure for bones and muscles.
quiz.4.prompt: What is the NASA umbrella term for eye changes associated with long-duration spaceflight?
quiz.4.explanation: Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) includes changes in eye shape and the optic nerve.
quiz.5.prompt: What is the main reason radiation exposure is lower on the ISS in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) compared to deep space?
quiz.5.choices.1: Attenuation by Earth's magnetic field and the spacecraft hull
quiz.5.choices.2: It can be neutralized by exercise
quiz.5.choices.3: It disappears if you drink water
quiz.5.explanation: LEO provides significant shielding from the magnetic field and the spacecraft hull. However, exposure is not zero; during Extravehicular Activities (EVA), astronauts are outside this shield.
quiz.6.prompt: Which circulatory change requires particular attention immediately after return?
quiz.6.choices.1: 1/6 G gravity like the Moon continues
quiz.6.choices.2: Orthostatic hypotension and reduced orthostatic tolerance
quiz.6.explanation: Circulation that readjusted in orbit may fail to maintain blood pressure when standing up in 1 G gravity.
quiz.7.prompt: Why do official fire protection guidelines consider combustion products particularly dangerous?
quiz.7.choices.3: Because they can become immediately harmful in a closed atmosphere with limited escape routes
quiz.7.explanation: The OCHMO fire guidelines state that in an environment with limited evacuation options and a fragile atmosphere, combustion products can immediately threaten life.
quiz.8.prompt: Which of the following is NOT included in the five primary hazards?
quiz.8.explanation: The official five hazards are gravity, distance, radiation, isolation and confinement, and hostile/closed environments.
quiz.9.prompt: Which muscles are most prone to atrophy in microgravity?
quiz.9.explanation: Anti-gravity muscles in the legs and trunk, which previously supported posture, are deemed unnecessary and prone to atrophy.
quiz.10.prompt: Which allocation strategy is likely to fail in a 180-day plan?
quiz.10.choices.2: Maximizing aerobic training while abandoning resistance training
quiz.10.explanation: Bones and muscles require resistance loading. Maximizing a single metric can silently increase other risks.
quiz.11.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes how NASA frames isolation and confinement?
quiz.11.choices.1: Ignored because it does not occur on Earth
quiz.11.choices.3: One of the five hazards and a mission risk
quiz.11.explanation: Isolation and confinement are official primary hazards, while behavioral health is an operational safety item.
quiz.12.prompt: Which of the following does this lesson list as a daily preventive measure in a closed environment?
quiz.12.choices.2: Keeping a fire burning at all times
quiz.12.explanation: In a closed atmosphere, daily management of CO2, humidity, and cleanliness serves as primary prevention for headaches, microbial growth, and fire risk.
quiz.13.prompt: Which of the following is an appropriate operational response to solar particle events?
quiz.13.choices.1: Check the forecast, delay EVAs, and retreat to a heavily shielded area
quiz.13.choices.2: Throwing water on it will make it disappear
quiz.13.choices.3: Ignore it and do not change the plan
quiz.13.explanation: Solar particle events require decisions ranging from hours to days. In deep space, particularly, sheltering and plan changes are the countermeasures for survival.
quiz.14.prompt: Which of the following does this lesson cite as a leading background factor for SANS?
quiz.14.choices.2: Fluid shift toward the head and pressure relationships in the eyes and skull
quiz.14.choices.3: Number of joints in the Canadian Arm
quiz.14.explanation: Fluid shift toward the head and associated pressure relationships are central to leading hypotheses regarding changes in eye shape and the optic nerve.
quiz.15.prompt: Which of the following does this lesson establish as a pass condition for health management?
quiz.15.choices.3: The spacecraft and ground medical teams viewing the same measurements
quiz.15.explanation: Countermeasures only work when they are reflected in calendars and logs. Missing measurements are a risk in themselves, as the absence of data is the risk.
glossary.0.description: Changes in gravity, distance from Earth, radiation, isolation and confinement, and hostile/closed environments. The official framework by which HRP bundles risks.
glossary.1.description: The phenomenon in microgravity where fluid moves from the legs toward the head. It simultaneously affects facial appearance, circulation, eyes, and the vestibular system.
glossary.2.description: A general term summarizing changes in eye shape and the optic nerve associated with long-duration spaceflight.
glossary.3.description: The resistance exercise device on the ISS. It is central to countermeasures for bone and anti-gravity muscles.
glossary.4.description: A condition after return where blood pressure cannot be maintained upon standing, causing symptoms such as darkening of vision.
glossary.5.description: High-energy particles from the galaxy. They cannot be completely stopped by the spacecraft hull and are particularly problematic in deep space.
glossary.6.description: Increases in particle radiation associated with solar activity. They necessitate operational decisions such as delaying EVAs and retreating to shelter.
glossary.7.description: A NASA program that researches health and performance risks in spaceflight and designs countermeasures.
glossary.8.description: A medical officer who supervises crew health from the ground, connecting daily measurements with emergency decision-making.
